Turf around an Oakland pool cage

Turf beside a pool or inside a screen enclosure in Oakland is priced at the residential range, $8–$18 a square foot, typically $10–$16, as of September 2026. Newer pool-cage homes at Longleaf and Briley Farm and older lanais closer to downtown need different edge details even though the price range is identical.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Glue-down edges where turf meets a pool deck

Inside a screen enclosure on an Oakland lot, turf meets the pool deck's concrete directly, with no soil to anchor a nailed perimeter into. That edge gets bonded with adhesive instead, and a thin drainage underlay goes beneath the turf so water from pool splash-out or a hosed-off deck has somewhere to go rather than sitting against the concrete. This detail is the same whether the cage is a decade old near downtown Oakland or finished last year at Briley Farm.

Why a pool quote often carries two separate turf line items

A Oakland property getting both a glued lanai floor and an open deck border should see those priced as two distinct line items on the same quote rather than one blended per-square-foot number, since the underlay, adhesive, and labor for a glued slab application cost differently than rock, compaction, and staked edges for an open border. A homeowner comparing two quotes for the same combined project should check that both bids split the work the same way; a quote that bundles everything into one number makes it harder to tell which area is driving most of the cost.

Say you have a 450 sq ft lanai surround

Say you have a 450 sq ft strip of turf planned around a screened pool at a Briley Farm home, replacing a paver border the builder left as dirt. At Oakland's typical residential range of $10 to $16 a square foot, that comes to about $4,500 to $7,200, with the glue-down edge along the pool deck and the drainage underlay both included in that figure rather than billed separately. An older in-town lanai needing the deck releveled first would price toward the higher end for the extra prep.

Newer construction changes the surrounding grade, not the edge detail

A Longleaf or Briley Farm pool-cage home usually has the lanai poured level with a clean grade already sloping away from the house, so the turf portion outside the cage is typically a straightforward strip rather than a project needing much regrading. An older in-town lot with a lanai added years after the original house sometimes has a deck that settled slightly, which we check with a level before assuming the drainage still falls the right direction.

What a wall of pool-cage sliders can do to the turf below

Large sliding glass doors are common on Oakland pool homes, and a low-emissivity coating on that much glass can reflect enough concentrated sunlight to soften turf directly in its path, since polyethylene blades start to give around 175 to 200°F under that kind of focused heat. The damage shows up as a scorched patch shaped by the reflection angle rather than by foot traffic, which is often the first clue it is glare and not wear. Checking a west- or south-facing wall of sliders before laying turf close to it avoids relocating a section later.

Why washed rock matters most where concrete meets soil

Rainfall that hits a pool deck's concrete has nowhere to go but sideways, onto whatever soil border sits at the cage's edge, so a Oakland lot's washed, open-graded crushed rock does more work at that transition than it does in the middle of an open lawn. Unwashed fill would let fines settle and bind right where the extra volume arrives first, turning a narrow strip into the one part of the yard that stays soggy after every storm. The state's rule that subgrade material be washed before installation exists for exactly this kind of concentrated flow, not just ordinary rain falling evenly across a yard.

Low-E glass near a pool cage is worth a look either way

Pool cages sit close to the house, and a west- or south-facing window with low-emissivity glass can reflect enough concentrated sun to soften turf several feet away, regardless of which Oakland neighborhood the home is in. Checking that reflection path before installation is a five-minute step that avoids a scorched patch showing up in the first full summer. How a melted patch actually happens goes through the low-E glass problem in more detail, and the pool and lanai turf guide covers glue-down edge work beyond what fits on this page. The same reflection check applies equally on a screen enclosure in Horizon West or Winter Garden.

Building a border and a glued floor as one sequenced job

When a Oakland property gets both an open deck border and a glued lanai floor at the same visit, the rock base for the border goes in and compacts first, before the slab gets pressure washed for the glue-down section, so dust and loose fines from the soil work do not land on a clean, prepped slab. Compacting the border early also gives that section time to settle while the crew finishes prepping and gluing the floor, rather than rushing both areas to be ready on the same afternoon. The two areas finish on the same day even though they are built in a different order.

Watching infill near the splash zone specifically

Coated sand or zeolite infill along the section of a Oakland border closest to the water depletes faster than infill further back, since regular hose rinsing and pool splash both wash a small amount out with every use, on top of whatever a summer storm contributes. Checking depth in that specific stretch every few months, rather than assuming the whole yard wears evenly, catches a thinning spot before it shows as a bare-looking patch in the exact area guests and family see most often. Topping off just that section is a smaller job than waiting for the whole border to look thin.

Questions people ask

Does turf inside a screen enclosure still need the 10-ft waterbody setback?

No. That setback applies to a natural or man-made waterbody like Lake Apopka or Johns Lake, not to a swimming pool, so a pool-cage lanai isn't affected by it.

Can turf go directly over an existing paver pool deck?

Usually yes, with a drainage layer and glue-down edges rather than nails, since pavers don't need to be removed first. We'd still check the paver base isn't already holding water before installing over it.
